systems.name: Vision & sensing
systems.summary: A humanoid must estimate its surroundings and its own body at the same time.
systems.how: Cameras provide information about objects, surfaces and motion. Joint-position sensing supplies proprioception: an estimate of where the limbs are. Contact and force feedback add information that an image can miss, such as whether a grasp is slipping.
systems.why: Recognizing a cup is only a first step. The robot also needs an actionable estimate of where it is, how it can be reached and what may change during contact. Occlusion, reflections, lighting and moving people complicate that estimate.
systems.tesla: Tesla’s stated engineering scope includes perception and physical interaction. Its published material does not provide a complete, final production sensor bill of materials here.
systems.boundary: This overview explains the roles of sensing. The diagram marks a topic, not the verified location of a particular production camera.

systems.name: Hands & touch
systems.summary: Dexterity is an interaction between mechanics, sensing and control.
systems.how: Tendons can transmit actuator force through a compact hand. Finger geometry and compliant surfaces shape the contact; tactile sensing can help detect pressure or slip. A successful grasp requires enough force to hold an object without crushing or damaging it.
systems.why: A rigid box, soft fabric and a slippery cylinder demand different contact strategies. Tendon wear, routing friction, protection, repair and repeatable assembly all matter when a hand has to work repeatedly rather than perform one showcase grasp.
systems.tesla: Tesla’s hand manufacturing role specifically describes tendons, tactile sensors and soft goods. Those are development areas, not a complete production hand specification.
systems.boundary: A degree of freedom is an independently describable motion. It is not a success-rate measure, and finger joint count need not equal actuator count.

systems.name: Actuators & joints
systems.summary: Motors and transmissions must produce useful force without making the robot too heavy or inefficient.
systems.how: An electric motor produces rotation. A transmission can trade speed for output torque; a screw mechanism can translate rotation into linear motion. Feedback from sensors allows a controller to regulate joint behavior rather than merely send an open-loop command.
systems.why: More gearing can increase available torque while affecting speed, friction and the inertia felt at the joint. Heat, mechanical play, packaging, maintenance and how a joint responds to an unexpected contact are part of the same engineering trade-off.
systems.tesla: Tesla has shown successive hardware revisions. The illustration is a generic motor-and-transmission explanation, not a cutaway of a proprietary Tesla actuator.
systems.boundary: An attractive motion clip does not disclose the torque-speed curve, continuous thermal limit or service life of a joint.

systems.name: Balance & locomotion
systems.short: Every step is a control problem.
systems.summary: Walking and carrying cannot be treated as entirely separate skills.
systems.how: The feet exchange forces with the floor. Moving a leg changes the available contacts; reaching or carrying changes the motion and loading of the whole body. A controller must coordinate those changes while respecting reach, friction and actuator limits.
systems.why: A smooth floor, a slippery patch and a stair are different contact problems. Quasi-static balance can be explained with a support region, but dynamic walking also depends on momentum and timing. A simple center-of-mass sketch is not a complete walking controller.
systems.tesla: Tesla’s overview identifies balance and navigation as necessary software capabilities. Public walking sequences demonstrate motion in their shown conditions; they do not establish universal terrain handling.
systems.boundary: The principle diagram explains contact and balance. It is not a Tesla simulation or a measured stability envelope.

systems.name: Learning & control
systems.summary: Training a behavior and deciding how it is controlled during a demo are different questions.
systems.how: Demonstrations can provide examples of how to act. Training adjusts a policy from data; at deployment, a controller uses observations to choose actions. Runtime teleoperation instead places a human in the control loop. A system can also combine autonomous behavior with occasional assistance.
systems.why: Good performance on familiar examples is not enough. A robot needs to handle variation, recover when something goes wrong and operate within a defined task and safety envelope. The evaluation must say what help, resets or prior setup were required.
systems.tesla: Tesla describes end-to-end learned sorting in its 2023 film, and its data-collection roles describe human motion-capture work. Neither statement establishes that every public demo is autonomous.
systems.boundary: This loop is an explanatory model. It does not claim Tesla uses another company’s published VLA architecture or disclose a proprietary network size.

systems.name: Power & durability
systems.short: A useful shift, not just a good clip.
systems.summary: Energy, heat, wear and repairability determine how long a robot can do useful work.
systems.how: A battery supplies motors, computing and auxiliaries. Repeated motion creates electrical and mechanical losses that appear as heat. Load, speed, pauses and the task sequence affect average power; charging time and service interruptions affect operational availability.
systems.why: A factory needs predictable output and recovery procedures, not simply a headline battery figure. Hands, joints, covers and sensors must survive repeated contact. Safe shutdown, fault detection, training for operators and maintenance access are part of deployment.
systems.tesla: The Q3 call identifies durability and continued hardware refinement as open work. Tesla’s 2.3 kWh disclosure was about the 2022 prototype; it is not used here to predict a current robot’s runtime.
systems.boundary: No independently verified full-shift uptime, final production battery capacity or current certified runtime is established by this guide.

faqs.question: What is Optimus?
faqs.answer: Tesla’s humanoid robot. Tesla’s stated goal is a general-purpose machine for work that is repetitive, dangerous or unwanted. It is now in early production in Fremont, California, but Tesla has not shown it doing a full working day for a customer.

faqs.question: Is Optimus in production?
faqs.answer: Tesla says yes: its Q3 2026 update reports that production began on its high-volume Fremont line and calls the output “the first production-quality bots” it has made. It has not said how many. In July, Tesla said early builds would go to its Optimus Academy to collect training data.

faqs.question: When can I buy one?
faqs.answer: Not yet. On the Q3 2026 call, Musk said he expects deliveries to companies outside Tesla around the end of 2027, with industrial users first. Home robots come later as production grows. These are targets, not dates.

faqs.question: How much will Optimus cost?
faqs.answer: Tesla has not published a price. Musk has given aspirations: under $20,000 at high volume (2022) and $20,000 to $30,000 at scale (2024). In October 2026, Tesla’s finance chief said cost was trending toward where Tesla expects Cybercab costs to land, adding it was too early to say it was there.

faqs.question: What is Gen 3?
faqs.answer: Tesla’s January 2026 update called Gen 3 “our first design meant for mass production”, with a new hand. Not a Tesla App reports that the Fremont line builds that design; Tesla has not formally unveiled it. Renders leaked from Tesla’s app in September 2026 and are unconfirmed.

faqs.question: How dexterous are the hands?
faqs.answer: Tesla described 11 degrees of freedom per hand in 2022 and for Gen 2 in 2023, with touch sensing on every finger. The production Gen 3 hand is reported at 22. Musk said in October 2026 that the hand is still being refined, and Tesla engineer Konstantinos Laskaris called it “one of the most challenging hardware areas”.

faqs.question: How tall and heavy is it?
faqs.answer: The only published height is from the 2021 concept: 5 ft 8 in (173 cm) and 125 lb (57 kg). Gen 2 was said to be 10 kg lighter than its predecessor. Tesla has not published Gen 3 dimensions.

faqs.question: Is it autonomous or remotely controlled?
faqs.answer: It depends on the demonstration. Tesla described sorting and cell handling as autonomous, and Musk said the 2025 kung-fu clip was AI, not teleoperation. Musk said the 2024 shirt folding was not autonomous, and Bloomberg reported human help for some We, Robot interactions. The archive below labels each case.

faqs.question: How does Optimus learn?
faqs.answer: Ashok Elluswamy, who leads Tesla’s AI software, said in October 2026 that Optimus has to learn by watching people do a task and then practising it, because, unlike the car fleet, there is no exoskeleton for people to get into and puppet the robot. Tesla also hires operators to record motion-capture data.

faqs.question: Does it run the car’s FSD software?
faqs.answer: It shares Tesla’s vision and computer work, but a humanoid also has to control balance, contact and dozens of joints. Musk says the next computer, AI5, is needed because Optimus has far more degrees of freedom than a car, and expects it in Optimus around April 2027.

faqs.question: Who runs the program?
faqs.answer: Ashok Elluswamy, who also leads Tesla’s Autopilot software, took responsibility for Optimus when Milan Kovac left in June 2025.

faqs.question: How does it compare with other humanoids?
faqs.answer: Others are further along in some ways. Agility’s Digit works at named customers, 1X takes deposits for a home robot, Unitree lists a robot from $13.5K, and Boston Dynamics showed a production Atlas bound for Hyundai. Tesla’s distinctive bet is scale: a line designed for a million robots a year.

faqs.question: Why a humanoid rather than a robot arm?
faqs.answer: A human-shaped robot can in principle use spaces and tools built for people. That flexibility costs more joints, balance and contact problems. A fixed arm is often better for one well-defined station.

faqs.question: How is this guide updated?
faqs.answer: It is an edited guide, not live factory data. The review date shows when every source was last checked. New filings, films and disclosures are added after review, and corrections are noted on the page.

credit.title: Tesla Optimus Gen 3
credit.author: Michael
credit.changes: Cut into 17 parts at the joints, simplified, textures re-encoded as WebP and geometry compressed by Supercharged Daily.

parts.name: Outer shell
parts.desc: Covers protect the joints, wiring and actuators and give the robot its shape. This exterior comes from a fan-made model; it resembles Gen 2 more than the unrevealed Gen 3.
parts.how: In the exploded view each cover slides away from its joint so the parts underneath show. Gen 3 renders found in Tesla’s app show sealed joint covers; Tesla has not confirmed them.
facts: Exterior by Michael on Sketchfab, CC BY 4.0

parts.name: Head and face plate
parts.desc: A smooth helmet with a dark face plate. The cameras sit behind the plate rather than in visible eyes.
parts.how: Gen 2 added a neck with two degrees of freedom, so the head can turn and nod to look at the task.

parts.name: Cameras
parts.desc: Optimus sees with cameras, using vision networks that Tesla adapted from its driving software.
parts.how: Tesla engineers described networks running on the robot’s camera streams at AI Day 2022. The two modules shown here are illustrative; Tesla has not published a camera count or placement.

parts.name: Central computer
parts.desc: “Also in our torso, we have our central computer,” Tesla said in 2022, with wireless connectivity, audio and hardware-level security.
parts.how: Keeping compute and power distribution at the centre of the body cuts wiring to the limbs. Musk expects the next chip, AI5, in Optimus around April 2027.

parts.name: Battery pack
parts.desc: A 2.3 kWh pack that Tesla said is “about a full day’s worth of work”. It sits in the middle of the torso: “it is the torso.”
parts.how: The battery electronics are integrated on a single board inside the pack. Tesla has not published a Gen 3 capacity.
facts: Electronics on one board in the pack

parts.name: Neck
parts.desc: Two small actuators turn and tilt the head.
parts.how: Tesla listed a 2-DoF actuated neck among the Gen 2 upgrades in December 2023.

parts.name: Rotary actuators
parts.desc: Fourteen rotary units: six at the shoulders, two at the wrists, four at the hips and two in the waist.
parts.how: Tesla described a bespoke permanent-magnet motor, a strain-wave gear, a cross-roller bearing, three integrated sensors and a mechanical clutch. The per-joint split comes from industry analysis of the AI Day layout.

parts.name: Linear actuators
parts.desc: Fourteen push-pull units: two at the elbows, four at the wrists, two at the hips, two at the knees and four at the ankles.
parts.how: Each uses planetary rollers and an inverted planetary screw, which Tesla said gives efficiency, compactness and durability. The strongest is “very tightly packaged in the knee”.

parts.name: Hands
parts.desc: Six actuators and 11 degrees of freedom per hand in 2022, with fingers “driven by metallic tendons that are both flexible and strong”.
parts.how: An in-hand controller drives the fingers and reads their sensors, and a clutch lets the hand hold an object without powering the motors. Not a Tesla App reports 22 degrees of freedom for the Gen 3 hand.

parts.name: Feet
parts.desc: Force and torque sensing in each foot tells the controller how weight is spread as the robot walks.
parts.how: Gen 2 added foot force/torque sensing, articulated toe sections and human-like foot geometry, per Tesla’s December 2023 film.

parts.name: Power and data
parts.desc: Cables carry power and signals from the torso to every actuator.
parts.how: Tesla said it chose to “centralize both our power distribution and our compute to the physical center of the platform” and reduce wiring at the extremities.
facts: Power and compute at the centre
Less wiring in hands and feet
